title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Brownfield.ai, Scout (ScoutCities), LandGate, Enverus Site & Screen. White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k.

title: Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning
one_liner: Producers call the vet before they call the state. Anonymized weekly counts of abortions, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and respiratory clusters are a leading indicator that traders, insurers and packers will pay for.
customer: Buyers: cattle and feeder analytics desks, market advisory and commodity funds, packer and feedlot risk managers, livestock and dairy insurers or reinsurers, animal health company territory teams, and state animal health boards (contracts or grants). Suppliers are participating rural vets, who get free early regional alerts and a small revenue share.
problem: Official disease data lags by weeks because it waits on lab confirmation, and ranchers hesitate to report to the state because a quarantine costs them money. Screwworm was confirmed in a Texas calf in June 2026 after roughly 60 years without a US case, and H5N1 in dairy cattle was spreading for months before detection in 2024. Cattle futures at record prices with a 70-year low herd move violently on rumor, and nobody has a systematic ground-level feed.
solution: A 30-second end-of-week SMS or one-tap tally where each vet reports counts by syndrome (abortion clusters, navel or wound maggots, sudden deaths, neurological, respiratory, milk drops) and ZIP3 or county. Counts are aggregated with k-anonymity (no client identity, minimum practice thresholds) and compared to seasonal baselines. Outputs are a weekly 'Rural Vet Pulse' regional index, push alerts when a region deviates, and an API for institutional subscribers. Vets get the regional alerts free, which is the give-to-get hook.
why_now: New World screwworm has been confirmed in Texas and New Mexico since June 2026, with the first infested horse reported in September 2026, and movement restrictions plus sterile-fly shortages make the outbreak's trajectory the biggest driver of cattle risk. H5N1 in dairy is ongoing, federal animal health staffing is stretched, and academic syndromic surveillance systems exist in Europe (Netherlands, France, Great Britain) but I found no commercial equivalent built from US rural vet practices.
revenue_model: $2-10K per month per institutional data subscriber (analytics desks, insurers, packers), enterprise API tiers, sponsored regional alerts from animal health companies, state or regional government pilots, and a $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice.
non_obvious_insight: Ranchers under-report to the state because reporting costs them money, but they do not hide problems from their vet because they need the vet's drugs and help. The vet's phone is the earliest sensor in the system, and vets cannot share client data but can share counts. Contrarian point: the absence of calls is also a signal, because call volume drops when producers hide problems during a quarantine.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 large-animal practices in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Kansas and Nebraska through state VMA lists and large-animal vet Facebook groups. Build the weekly tally as a plain SMS survey, with no software integration. Publish a free regional weekly newsletter to the vets as the hook. Backtest screwworm lead time against USDA confirmation dates and pitch 3 market-advisory or cattle analytics shops for a $1-2K per month paid pilot.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SAVSNET / FAVSNET (University of Liverpool), Morrison Swine Health Monitoring Project (Univ. of Minnesota) and Swine Health Information Center (SHIC), Equine Disease Communication Center (US Equestrian), USDA APHIS / NAHLN and Texas Animal Health Commission (mandatory reporting). White space: Verdict basis: I found no commercial or non-commercial system that turns weekly counts from US large-animal (cattle) vet practices into a regional syndromic index sold to institutional buyers. I could not test that claim against Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch or Product Hunt, so treat it as unconfirmed on the startup side.

What exists today:
- Academic systems, mostly in Europe (SAVSNET/FAVSNET in the UK).
- A 2025 scoping review of 126 animal syndromic systems: 67 percent were still proof-of-concept, only 20 percent were fully operational, and it noted that even established systems are vulnerable to loss of funding. Operational ones were mostly government run. This is a nearby-review finding, not proof that nobody is building this in the US. Source: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40327964
- Free industry models such as MSHMP (swine) and the equine EDCC.
- Companion-animal practice data businesses (Animalytix, Vetsource).
- Government mandatory reporting, which now covers confirmed and suspected screwworm within 24 hours in Texas.

Unserved, specifically:
1. Pre-confirmation, syndromic, cattle-specific signals: abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and milk drops, at ZIP3 or county level, weekly. Government reporting only covers confirmed or suspected reportable disease.
2. A denominator and absence-of-calls signal that no current system produces.
3. A decision-grade product for private actors who face NWS movement restrictions and have no ground-level feed: sale barns, order buyers, feedlots, packers, insurers and animal health territory teams.

Structural risks that keep this a gap rather than open:
- Government and free alternatives (TAHC and USDA public case counts, EDCC-style free alerts) satisfy much of the need.
- Vets are legally obligated to report suspects to TAHC, so a private feed adds little for confirmed cases.
- Privacy and trade-implication concerns were the top barrier in an Australian stakeholder study (https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40037116).
- Selling vet-sourced early disease signals to commodity funds carries legal and ethics exposure (material non-public information, duty-to-report conflicts).

title: China-Asset Diligence Desk for Pharma BD
one_liner: A bilingual scientist-plus-software sprint that verifies China-sourced drug packages (raw data, GLP and CMC standing, ownership chain) in 72 hours for US buyers.
customer: Pharma BD&L teams, NewCo-building VCs, royalty funds and mid-cap biotechs in-licensing Chinese assets.
problem: About one-third of 2025 licensing spend involved China-sourced drugs (Jefferies) and the pace accelerated in 2026 (Lilly-InnoCare up to $3.35B, Merck-SciBrunch $2.1B). Diligence infrastructure looks thin (inference): data packages are in Chinese formats, raw-data and audit-trail norms differ, and CRO and CDMO GLP or GMP standing is hard to verify. BIOSECURE, enacted Dec 18, 2025, requires OMB to publish the list of biotechnology companies of concern by December 2026 and FAR rules follow, adding an ownership and supply-chain axis.
solution: A fixed-price 'Asset Verification Sprint'. LLM-assisted translation and structured extraction of study reports. Bilingual scientists spot-check raw data and audit trails. Verify CRO and CDMO inspection histories (NMPA, FDA, EMA) and check ownership chains against the BIOSECURE lists. Deliver a Western-format gap analysis for IND-enabling needs (GLP tox acceptability, CMC comparability).
why_now: Deal flow is at record levels, BIOSECURE list publication is due in about three months, and biopharma layoffs (15,000+) free bilingual ex-pharma scientists.
revenue_model: $25-70k per sprint, $150-300k annual retainers for NewCo-builder VCs, and supply-chain mapping as a second product once the BIOSECURE lists land.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is not legal or financial diligence. It is data literacy and tacit standards, for example what counts as GLP-grade raw data, and Western deal associates cannot read the packages. The same team and database serve a second product, supply-chain mapping, when the lists arrive.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-4 bilingual ex-pharma scientists. Price a $20k pilot sprint. Approach 5 NewCo VC platforms and 5 mid-size pharma BD heads. Build a CRO and CDMO inspection database from public regulator records.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Alacrita (biotech consulting network), Patsnap Synapse (AI drug asset due diligence reports), Pharmcube (Yaozhi / Pharma Insight consulting), Locust Walk / Banyan BioInnovations. White space: Nobody found sells what the idea specifies: a fixed-price, bilingual scientist-led verification of a China-sourced drug package's raw data and audit trails, GLP-tox acceptability for a US IND, CMC comparability, and CRO/CDMO standing, delivered as a Western-format gap memo for buyers with no China bench. What exists is adjacent. Data platforms (Pharmcube, Patsnap, Evaluate/Norstella) and AI screening do sourcing and public-data diligence. Investment banks (Locust Walk) and law firms (Sidley, Foley Hoag, Morgan Lewis) do deal access, legal and IP. General biotech consultancies (Alacrita) do generic diligence with no China raw-data focus. Redica sells inspection data. Patsnap's own sample report says binding deals still need source-data review, which points at the wedge. The underserved buyers are NewCo-building VCs below RA Capital or Banyan scale, mid-cap biotechs and royalty funds with no Shanghai presence. Two weaknesses to plan around: (1) the inspection database is a commodity (Redica, and the FDA has promised to publish more foreign-site inspection findings), and BIOSECURE list tracking overlaps with Kharon and Interos, so the moat has to be scientist judgment and trust, not software; (2) seller data access is a bottleneck. Locust Walk's CEO says 'getting data out of the company can be challenging', and China's data-export and human-genetic-resources rules (Morgan Lewis playbook) may block raw-data transfer. The 72-hour promise will be hard unless the seller supplies a data room. Coverage caveat: I could not run WebSearch (session budget exhausted), so I relied on Google News RSS, direct fetches of vendor sites and the YC directory. Stealth boutiques and Big-4 or CRO consulting units were not exhaustively checked.

title: Lender-Paid Calf Collateral Inspection and Lot Grading
one_liner: Sell independent day-3-to-6 lot grading to the feed, milk-replacer and ag-loan credit desks that finance calf raisers, as collateral inspection, so the party who really loses money on every dead calf pays for the measurement.
customer: Credit managers at regional feed and milk-replacer distributors that carry 30-90 day trade credit to calf ranches, and ag lenders and calf-ownership financing programs that lend against calf inventory. Wedge: one distributor with 15-40 non-integrated calf-raiser accounts and $2M or more in calf-related receivables. Raisers are the secondary beneficiary and pay through a loan-document inspection fee or through better credit terms.
problem: A 500-head lot of crossbred calves is now $500-750K of collateral, and the lender's monitoring is still a headcount and the raiser's own say-so. A bad intake lot with poor passive transfer can lose a large share of its calves within weeks (the parent's 10-25% raiser loss is unverified). My inference, to be validated in customer calls, is that the credit desk usually learns of it from a missed payment 30-60 days later. The lender cannot trust the raiser's self-reported Brix, and the raiser cannot prove to the lender that a bad lot was bad luck at intake rather than bad management. Nobody prices the biological quality of the collateral.
solution: For each new lot placed at a financed ranch, an independent tech samples 20 calves within 24-72 hours of arrival (day 3-6 of age), with custody-stamped tube and tag capture. Within 24 hours the credit desk receives a Lot Risk Grade (A-D) built from the Lombard tiers, with an expected 30-day loss band, taken from the published roughly 2x risk for failure of passive transfer at first and replaced by our own pooled data. Credit terms key off the grade: A lots get full limit and fast approval, C/D lots trigger a hold or a risk-sharing plan. The raiser gets a same-day early-warning call for D lots (isolate Poor calves, fluid and treatment protocol), so the inspection is a service to them rather than a tax. Year 2: a loss-outcome dataset licensed to reinsurers and MGAs.
why_now: Crossbred calf collateral per head has multiplied several times over versus a few years ago (beef-on-dairy went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to about 3.2M in 2024 per the parent, and calves have reached $1,500), so headcount-style monitoring that was fine at $100 a calf is negligent at $1,400. Cheap refractometers, phone custody capture and now a published grading standard make lot inspection cost about $1.50-2 a calf. The 2020 consensus tiers give lenders a common language for the first time.
revenue_model: $250-450 per lot inspected (about $1.50-2 per calf), billed to the lender or supplier and recoverable from the raiser as a collateral inspection fee, plus $150-300 a month per financed ranch for the monitoring dashboard. A ranch placing 300 calves a week is about 52 lots a year, or roughly $18K a year. A distributor with 40 accounts is about $700K a year. Later: loss-data license to insurers and reinsurers, and a per-lot fee for a lender-requested claims audit. Market ceiling on fees is modest but recurring, and the buyer's value (bad debt avoided) is a multiple of the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the most money at risk per dead calf is not in the room and is not the raiser. It is the credit provider. Collateral management (independent inspectors working for banks) is an old, boring industry that has never priced the biological quality of livestock. This makes the business independent of two weaknesses in the parent: it needs no buyer premium for graded calves, and it avoids warranty moral hazard because the customer prices and monitors credit rather than insuring loss.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: hold 20 short calls with credit managers at feed and milk-replacer distributors and ag loan officers in one dairy-dense county. Ask what they lose per year to calf-ranch defaults, how they learn of a bad lot, and whether collateral inspection fees are already collectible under their loan documents. Days 15-30: sign a free 60-day pilot with one distributor covering 6 friendly ranches. Two techs, about 12 lots a week, and a 24-hour grade report the credit manager marks up with what they would have changed. At day 60, compare grade against 30-day loss and any past-due behavior, then ask for a signed $300-a-lot agreement. Gate: the credit manager names annual avoided bad debt of at least 10x the annual fee. If lenders will not state a number, kill it. Before pitching, verify the loss-rate and market-size figures and check for existing livestock collateral inspection firms.
lineage: mutation of I0617 ('Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement. | How this version avoids them: Where Food Comes From sells claim verification to marketers, brands and packers. It has no lender product and does no per-lot sampling for credit decisions, so the buyer and the job are different. Calftech-style integrated ranches self-fund and self-monitor, so they are out of scope by design. This targets non-integrated raisers who have to prove intake quality to a lender, and independence is what makes an inspection valid collateral evidence. The $1 self-test objection disappears, because the lender is exactly the party who cannot accept the raiser's own test. There is no dependence on a graded-calf premium (the parent's weakest evidence) and no underwriting exposure. Vets who already test at herd checks work for the raiser and cannot serve as the lender's independent eyes.

title: Payable Bias Audit for Black Mass Sellers
one_liner: A fixed-price audit that measures, in euros per year, the systematic sampling bias between a black mass seller's protocol and its buyer's. The fix is then locked in as a sealed sample-of-record and a two-line contract clause.
customer: Wedge: independent mechanical pre-processors and EV/ESS dismantlers in Germany, Poland and Benelux. They sell roughly 300-3,000 t/yr of black mass (about EUR 1-8M/yr) to one or two hydromet buyers on a binding buyer-gate assay. About 40-60 such sellers exist in the corridor. The buyer of the audit is the owner, CFO or commercial director who signs the offtake contract, not the QA chemist. Gigafactory scrap desks come later, since they have in-house metallurgists and slow procurement.
problem: The parent sells noise reduction, but random sampling noise mostly nets out for a seller shipping 40-100 lots a year. What does not net out is systematic bias between two protocols. A grab from the top of a big bag or drum, an unrecorded moisture basis, and segregation of coarse Cu/Al foil against fine cathode powder all push in one direction on every lot, so bias moves money one way. A 3% payable bias on EUR 5M of annual sales is EUR 150k a year, invisible lot by lot. The umpire clause cannot catch it. Bureau Veritas's own umpire page (fetched this session) describes umpire work as its own analysis of samples, that is, a re-assay of the retained sample. If the retained sample carries the bias, the umpire confirms it. Sellers therefore concede, or split the difference, on lots they were systematically shorted on.
solution: Step 0 costs nothing. Ask the seller for 30-plus historical lots with its own dispatch assay and the buyer's settlement assay. A significant one-signed mean gap qualifies the prospect. It might be lab bias or sampling bias, and the audit separates the two. Step 1 is the Paired-Protocol Bias Audit, sold at EUR 20-30k. Over 8-10 lots, take three samples per lot: the seller's method, the buyer's documented method, and a Theory-of-Sampling incremental sample from a falling stream or drum auger, split by rotary divider into sealed triplicates. Blind full-digestion assays go to one accredited lab, with a 20% cross-check at a second. The deliverable is the bias with a confidence interval, the euros per year it costs, a Gy heterogeneity and sampling-variance statement, and a written seller Sampling Protocol of Record. Step 2 is a per-lot Sample-of-Record service using a portable kit of about EUR 15-25k (rotary divider, riffle splitters, balance, drying oven, inert glove bag). It gives sealed triplicates at load-out and a two-line clause: 'sample of record taken per Protocol v1, sampling variance not to exceed x% relative at 95%, retained split binds on dispute'. If the buyer refuses the clause, the seller holds the data to shop the volume to another recycler. No containerised station is built until an anchor customer pays for one.
why_now: Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, per the parent research), so sellers are already renegotiating counterparty terms and a new clause is on the table anyway. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 has been in force since 24 July 2025, and recyclers report annually to member-state authorities from 2026. Composition data for intermediate fractions such as black mass therefore has to be documented, which turns a written sampling protocol into a compliance artefact. Ni/Co price swings make each percentage point of payable worth more.
revenue_model: Audit fee of EUR 20-30k, with about EUR 10-12k of lab pass-through. Per-lot Sample-of-Record fee of EUR 900-1,800, or EUR 8-15 per tonne. Optional protocol licence to a buyer who wants to adopt the seller's protocol as its own. Year-1 target: 6 audits and 4 conversions at about 40 lots each, roughly EUR 350-400k revenue on about EUR 40k of kit. It is deliberately a small service business first, and the dataset of bias by protocol is the asset it builds.
non_obvious_insight: The value is the sign and size of the bias, not the reduction in variance. The party it costs is the natural buyer, and it is already identifiable from settlement history before any sampling. That makes the sales motion outbound and quantified (euros lost per year) instead of a vague accuracy pitch. A 'no bias found' result is also sellable, as a clean bill for lenders and counterparties. Because the umpire re-assays the same retained sample, no incumbent product is structured to detect the effect.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain a named senior sampling practitioner and an accredited partner lab. Anchor Protocol v1 to representative-sampling standards such as DS 3077 and, by analogy, ISO 12743 for concentrates. Both are recalled from memory, so verify. Build a one-page leak calculator from public payables and the seller's own settlement pairs. Weeks 2-3: send it to 40 named sellers in the DE/PL corridor and run the historical-pair test for every taker. Weeks 3-4: sign three audits at cost (about EUR 12k of pass-through each) in return for permission to publish anonymised results. Buy or lease a used rotary divider and portable kit. Go/no-go: at least 2 of 3 show a bias worth more than the audit fee, otherwise pivot to offspring 2 or 3.

Alex Stewart's site (fetched) does list representative sampling combined with analysis for recycled and electronic scrap, so the sampling itself is not the wedge. The wedge is a seller-side, euro-denominated bias audit with a stated sampling variance. That is a product the majors have a channel conflict selling, because the audit implicates the protocols their own crews run for the buyer. I found no evidence they publish sampling uncertainty for black mass, though SGS and Intertek pages could not be checked. ALS and Alex Stewart are supplier candidates for the assay leg. Multotec and Metso are suppliers of dividers. There is no capex race and no umpire-lab race.

title: WhatsApp Voice-Note Superintendent for Spec Builders
one_liner: A bilingual coordinator-plus-AI service that runs daily crew confirmations, headcounts and re-sequencing for a builder's two dozen subs over WhatsApp voice notes, priced per house.
customer: Small private and spec builders (20-300 homes a year) in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, and remodelers who juggle many subs.
problem: A typical home needs about two dozen subs. Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and one executive described 15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks. Builders learn a crew is not coming days too late. Project software requires English typing and logins, and workers are wary of anything that looks like tracking. Procore's 20 agents serve larger GCs.
solution: Foremen keep sending Spanish voice notes on WhatsApp. The system transcribes them, extracts headcount, phase status and photos, and updates the schedule. A nearshore bilingual coordinator confirms tomorrow's crews by 5 p.m., calls backup crews when there is a gap, and sends the builder one exception report each morning. Privacy by design: counts and progress only, no IDs or location.
why_now: ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026. Crews can shrink overnight (a Minnesota roofing crew went from 80 to 6). Multilingual speech models and the WhatsApp Business API are mature, and PM incumbents are focused on big GCs.
revenue_model: $300-500 per active house per month, or $3-6K per month per builder. One coordinator handles 25-40 houses, so gross margin is high.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not scheduling math, it is that the people who know whether tomorrow's crew is coming do not use the software. The interface must be the phone and language they already use. The daily headcount is the leading indicator, and knowing a day earlier lets a builder re-sequence trades instead of idling a foundation.
first_30_days: Sign 3 builders with 10-20 active houses each through a home builders association. Hire one bilingual coordinator. Run it manually with WhatsApp and a shared sheet, add speech-to-text in week 2, and document five saved crew-days.

White space: Research coverage was thin. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before my searches ran, so I had no search results at all. title: Keep-Warm: Preserving Power in Idle Plants
one_liner: Invert the database: instead of scoring dead plants once, sell a monthly service that keeps their electrical service alive and monitored, then turn 200 preserved shells into a right-of-first-offer inventory and, later, a balance-sheet powered-shell bank.
customer: Wedge: banks, special servicers and lenders holding real-estate-owned industrial plants, plus corporate owners of mothballed plants and county land banks, in the Mahoning Valley and Akron/Canton first. Later buyers: data-center, battery and manufacturing developers who pay for shells certified 'energized-ready'.
problem: An idle plant's electrical system is a wasting asset on a clock. Standard commercial property policies limit cover for vandalism, theft, water damage and sprinkler leakage once a building has been vacant for about 60 days (an assumption to verify with an insurance broker), copper theft and roof leaks wreck switchgear, utilities can pull service or reclassify accounts on idle meters, oil-filled transformers degrade, and permit fees and reports lapse. Residential-style property-preservation firms winterize and change locks, but nobody is paid to preserve amps. Owners find out the plant is worth far less than it was only when a buyer's electrician opens the gear two years later.
solution: Two tiers. 'Watch' at $650 per month: baseline electrician record (the Power Passport becomes the set-up fee), a $600 sensor kit (humidity, temperature, door, current clamps on the main service, cellular camera), quarterly thermography, and an insurer-facing monthly report. 'Warm' at $2,200 per month: monthly electrician visits, keep-energized management with the utility including minimum-bill and account status, annual transformer oil sampling, dehumidification, theft-alarm response and permit fee and report compliance. The continuous data produces an 'energized-ready' score, days to first power, and a verified time series no one-off inspection can match. Marketing and right-of-first-offer rights are bundled into the contract for owners who want a sale.
why_now: Low-cost cellular sensors and cameras collapsed to tens of dollars a unit. Vision models now read nameplates and gear photos cheaply, which cuts analyst hours per building. More industrial shells are going idle while buyers now pay a premium for existing power, so, for the first time, preserving the electrical system has a positive return.
revenue_model: Recurring: $650 or $2,200 per building per month plus a $2,500 baseline record; a carry-cost comparison shows a 300k sq ft idle plant costing an owner roughly $15k-$40k per month, so the service is 3-8% on top of existing carry. Gross margin about 50-55% at 10 buildings per electrician route. Insurer angle: partner with a vacant-property insurance managing general agent to turn monitoring into a rating credit, which can pay for itself. Scale path: 200 buildings on Warm and Watch is about $4M-$5M annual recurring revenue; the contract's right of first offer gives inventory to sell to buyers on a fee basis; a later fund of $50M-$100M exercises options on the best 20 shells, subdivides them into permitted 'factory condos' or powered shells and sells or leases at a premium. First 6 months: 5-8 paying buildings.
non_obvious_insight: The same service that stops the asset dying also builds the only dataset that matters: a time series of load, temperature, humidity and access on hundreds of idle industrial buildings, and exclusive access to a pipeline of them. That combination is a cornered resource plus a switching cost, defended by contracts and data history and not by scoring algorithms anyone can copy. The parent is a snapshot; this is the movie, and a monthly bill is a better business than a report.
first_30_days: Week 1: list 40 idle plants owned by banks, special servicers and land banks from county auditor and REO data in two metros; contact 8 REO and asset managers. Week 2: call two vacant-property insurance brokers and one managing general agent to test whether monitoring earns a premium credit or a vacancy-clause endorsement (the riskiest assumption). Weeks 3-4: sign three 90-day pilots on Watch at a waived set-up fee in exchange for a case study and marketing rights, install kits, and deliver the first insurer-facing report. Success test: one lender converts to $650 per month paid and one insurer or broker confirms a written premium credit or vacancy accommodation.

Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The business is recurring service revenue with a proprietary time series, so a funded data competitor would have to hire electricians and sign owner contracts to copy it, and the exclusive marketing rights become a cornered resource.

title: AI Exclusion Diff for Pro-Liability Renewals
one_liner: Forward a renewal quote or binder PDF and get, within 24 hours, a diff against the expiring policy, a breadth score for any new AI exclusion, and a client-ready gap letter. It is built for the professional-liability desk of independent agencies, and it also ranks competing quotes by exclusion breadth.
customer: The professional-services desk at independent agencies of 8-60 staff. That means the producer or account manager who handles 60-120 E&O, tech E&O, D&O, cyber and pro-services CGL renewals a year for architects and engineers, accountants, law firms, marketing and design agencies, and IT and software services firms. Much of their paper is surplus lines placed through wholesalers, which SERFF-based tools cannot see.
problem: AI exclusions on professional-liability paper are the broadest and most bespoke (Berkley's 'absolute' PC 51380, 'any AI' versus gen-AI only, vendor-supplied AI, BI/PD versus advertising injury, manuscript wording). They arrive buried in a stack of quote and binder PDFs, and the premium barely moves. The producer has about 10 minutes per renewal and no way to tell whether the exclusion is new, how wide it is, or whether it hits what the client actually does. Quandri and Zywave compare premium and limits. Patra checks 900+ points but is not AI-specific and does not diff against the expiring form. Filing trackers show what a carrier filed in a state, not what is attached to this client's policy.
solution: Intake is an email-in address with no AMS integration. The producer forwards the quote, binder or policy PDF plus the expiring policy. The output is a one-page report with five parts. (1) Diff: is an AI exclusion new, widened or unchanged versus expiring. (2) Breadth score of 0-5 across six dimensions: gen-AI only versus any AI, BI/PD versus advertising or personal injury, vendor-supplied AI, professional-services carve-outs, defence-cost treatment, and prior-acts effect. (3) A short 8-question client AI-use intake, which shows which of the client's real AI uses are now stranded. (4) A client-ready gap letter with a signed-acknowledgment page. (5) Quote-stage ranking: when the producer holds 2-4 competing quotes, it ranks them by exclusion breadth and drafts the exact carve-back request to send back, for example 'replace any-AI with gen-AI-only and carve out vendor-supplied AI'. Public filings (Trades Coverage, Certian, Gridex) are used only as a free auto-labeller for known forms. Delivery in the first months is LLM extraction plus a retired E&O underwriter reviewing every report. The output is a PDF plus JSON that files into Epic or Zywave as an attachment, so the product is a partner add-on and not a rival dashboard.
why_now: Renewals dated 1 Jan 2027 are the first big cycle after the ISO CG 40 47/40 48 forms and Berkley's absolute exclusion, and those quotes reach producers in Nov-Dec 2026, which is now. Trade press and associations (IA Magazine on 9 Sep 2026, Big I, Agents United) are telling agencies to review renewals for AI exclusions, but they give no tooling. Zywave's Advisor Agent, in early access since June 2026, is teaching agencies to expect renewal triage, and it does not read endorsements. Long-context PDF extraction on scanned binders is now cheap and reliable enough to do the classification at a cost of about $1 per document.
revenue_model: Pay per renewal at $150 for a standard quote diff and $450 for a multi-policy or manuscript diff. A $600/month plan includes 20 diffs. A $500 concierge audit on an agency's five largest accounts is the entry offer. Unit economics: about $1 of inference plus 15 minutes of reviewer time at about $60/hour gives roughly 85% gross margin on a $150 diff. This is my estimate: 1,000-2,000 US agencies run a real professional-liability desk, at 80 renewals a year that is $12-24k per agency, so 100 agencies is about $1.2-2.4M ARR. Referral revenue from affirmative markets is optional upside, and nothing depends on it, which answers the judges' doubt about the 10-15% commission.
non_obvious_insight: The thing a producer pays for is the ask, not the detection. Manuscript AI exclusions are negotiable, and a diff that says 'this wording is broader than the same carrier's competitor quote, ask for this replacement' turns a defensive letter into a shopping and negotiation tool that wins the account. The E&O-fear trigger also does not depend on the duty-to-advise law, which is weak in most states. Agencies that sell 'annual coverage reviews' assume a duty, and the signed acknowledgment turns that exposure into a documented file. The moat is not the public filings database. It is a labelled corpus of issued forms as attached to real quotes, including surplus lines, with outcome labels showing which carve-backs carriers actually granted. That corpus grows with every diff, and nobody can scrape it.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: recruit 10 pro-services-heavy agencies through LinkedIn and state agent-association contacts, and hire a retired professional-liability underwriter at 10 hours a week to write the 6-dimension rubric. Days 8-20: collect each agency's last 3 renewals for its 5 biggest pro-liability accounts (about 150 documents) and run the manual-plus-LLM diff. Measure the hit rate, meaning the share of renewals containing an AI exclusion the producer had not flagged. Proceed if it is 30% or more, and treat under 15% as the kill signal. Days 15-30: sell the $500 concierge audit and convert each agency to per-diff pricing for its live Nov-Dec 1/1 renewals. Publish the breadth scale v0.1 with 20 anonymised specimen forms as free content, and open a developer-partner conversation with Zywave and the Epic marketplace.

title: Agency E&O Insurers Fund AI-Exclusion File Reviews
one_liner: The insurers and endorsed programs that cover insurance agencies pay to put an AI-exclusion review and a client-acknowledgment file behind every commercial renewal their insured agencies handle. It is funded as loss control, in the way cyber insurers fund security scans, and the agency pays little or nothing.
customer: Payer: underwriting and program managers at insurance-agency E&O carriers and MGAs, and the state independent-agent associations that endorse an E&O program to their members. Users: the insured agencies with 5-100 staff. Buyer chain: the party who bears the cost of failure-to-warn claims pays, and the party who does the work receives the tool.
problem: Agency E&O carriers will pay defence costs and settlements when a client discovers, after an AI-caused loss, that the renewal quietly excluded AI and nobody told them. The exclusions are silent (the premium barely changes), they arrive in mass on 1/1/2027 renewals, and the claims will surface in 2027-2029. Even where the duty to advise is weak, defence costs are incurred anyway. Today these carriers have only PDF advisories and webinars, no data on whether any insured agency did anything, and no view of aggregate exposure across their book.
solution: A white-labelled program, called the 'Exclusion File' in the carrier's brand, with three parts. (1) Agency workflow: the agency forwards the renewal quote or policy PDF and receives the diff, the breadth score and a gap letter. The client e-signs an acknowledgment, either accepting the exclusion or asking for affirmative cover or a negotiated carve-back. Everything is stored in an audit-ready vault, which is the classic E&O defence of documented advice. (2) Carrier dashboard: the share of insured agencies enrolled, the share of commercial renewals reviewed, unresolved acknowledgments, and anonymised aggregate exclusion prevalence and breadth by line and by carrier form. It shows the carrier's own exposure. (3) Underwriting hook: a supplemental question on the E&O application, 'Do you review renewals for AI exclusions and retain client acknowledgments?', and an optional rate credit or deductible break for agencies that complete the program on 90% or more of their commercial renewals. The diff engine underneath is the same as in the sharpened offspring, so the marginal build cost is the vault, the e-sign flow and the dashboard.
why_now: The first large exclusion cycle is 1 Jan 2027, so an E&O carrier that acts in Q4 2026 has a defensible risk-control story before any claims exist. Trade and association content already urges agencies to review renewals (Big I on the Verisk rollout, Agents United, IA Magazine on 9 Sep 2026), so the carriers' insureds are being asked to act with no help. Cyber insurers that fund scans and security tooling for insureds have made the loss-control-for-premium-credit model familiar to underwriters. Agency E&O is a concentrated market with few carriers and programs, so a small number of decisions covers a lot of insured agencies.
revenue_model: The carrier or program pays $600-1,500 per enrolled agency per year, plus $25-60k per year for a quarterly AI-exclusion exposure report for its underwriters and reinsurers. The agency pays a $49-99 copay per diff, or nothing where the carrier sponsors it fully. An association that endorses the program takes an endorsed-vendor fee of 10-15% of agency revenue, which is how associations already monetise vendor programs. As an illustration: a carrier insuring 1,500 agencies, 20% enrolled at $900 each, is about $270k a year, plus the data subscription. These figures are estimates to be tested in pilot.
non_obvious_insight: The E&O insurer is the only party in the chain that pays whether or not a court finds a duty to advise, so it does not care about the legal debate that weakens the broker-side pitch. The distribution lever is also the E&O application. Once the supplemental question is on the form, agencies need a compliant answer every year, and this program becomes the standard way to give one. The same carrier-funded logic scales to the next silent-exclusion wave, whether PFAS, cyber war, biometric or another, so the customer can renew and expand on the same integration.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write a 2-page memo for underwriters with three concrete failure-to-warn fact patterns on 1/1/2027 renewals and a list of the largest agency E&O carriers, MGAs and association-endorsed programs. Book calls through LinkedIn and state association staff, and aim for 5 calls. Days 10-25: offer 3 state associations a free 45-minute webinar, 'AI exclusions on your Jan 1 renewals', which is a cheap way to capture 100+ agencies. Sign 10-25 of them as a pilot cohort using the concierge diff. Days 20-30: take the pilot cohort's hit-rate numbers (how many renewals had a new AI exclusion the agency had not flagged) back to the carriers and associations as a pilot pitch. Ask for a 3-month pilot at about $15k for 25 agencies, or an association endorsement. Carrier cycles run 3-6 months, so the association route generates the first revenue.

title: Vet-Verified Herd Exposure and Outbreak Index
one_liner: Rural large-animal vets sell two things from one app: borrower-approved, chute-side verified herd counts for ag lenders, and anonymized weekly syndrome tallies whose denominators come from those counts, giving lenders, insurers and traders a true disease-rate signal.
customer: Community banks and Farm Credit lenders (verified herd reports), livestock insurers and reinsurers, cattle analytics desks, packers and feedlot risk managers, animal-health company territory teams, and state animal health boards. Supply side is 25-50 large-animal practices.
problem: Lenders can't verify how many cows exist or where they are, and vets sit on that data unused. Vets can see outbreaks weeks before the state does but their tallies have no denominator, so a count of abortions means nothing without knowing how many bred cows are in that ZIP3. Vets also refuse to police clients, so neither product works if it feels like surveillance.
solution: One vet app and one relationship. At preg-check and weaning, the vet logs every head by EID or tag scan, age class, pregnancy status and location. The borrower approves sharing with a single tap, and the lender gets a timestamped Verified Herd Report. Every week the same vet sends a 30-second SMS tally by syndrome (abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths, respiratory, milk drops), aggregated with k-anonymity. Outputs are a per-1,000-head regional index for subscribers, a lender portfolio dashboard with a regional disease overlay, and later an exposure-plus-hazard dataset for livestock insurers.
why_now: Fall preg-check season is live now, so the first verified counts can be collected this quarter. Screwworm and other disease anxiety has traders, insurers and state boards asking for leading indicators. The vet-as-verifier trust position is the same in both products, so one sales conversation with each practice covers both.
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split about 50/50 with the vet, charged to borrower or lender. $500-2,000 per month lender portfolio dashboards. $2-10k per month institutional subscribers for the outbreak index. $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice on top of the per-head fee. Later, data licensing and pricing support for livestock disease cover.
non_obvious_insight: Verified herd inventory is an exposure layer, and vet syndrome tallies are a hazard layer, which is exactly what an insurer needs to price livestock disease cover. Neither layer alone can be underwritten. The denominator also lets the index read the 'absence of calls' signal properly, since call volume per 10,000 head falling during a quarantine looks different from a quiet region. Two revenue streams turn vets from reluctant borrowers' auditors into advocates: verification is borrower-initiated and tallies are anonymized, so the conflict-of-interest objection goes away.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 rural practices in TX, OK, KS or NE that each do thousands of head of fall preg-checks, and pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders via the state bankers' association ag committee. Run about 10 borrower pilots at $2/head with a form-based app and a PDF report. In parallel, start the plain SMS weekly tally with 25 practices and a free regional newsletter as the give-to-get hook. Backtest screwworm lead time against official confirmation dates and pitch 3 analytics shops for a $1-2k per month paid pilot.
lineage: hybrid of I0338 + I0199 (Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders + Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning). Why stronger: Cow counts alone are a small per-head fee and the outbreak signal alone is a free-data-for-nothing pitch to vets. Combined, vets earn twice from one workflow, the outbreak index gets denominators nobody else has, and the herd data gains a hazard overlay, which opens the much larger livestock insurance and reinsurance buyer that neither product reaches alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.\n\nWhat the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.\n\nThe unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.\n\nStructural weaknesses to be skeptical of:\n- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.\n- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.\n- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.\n- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.\n- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SAVSNET / FAVSNET (University of Liverpool), Morrison Swine Health Monitoring Project (Univ. of Minnesota) and Swine Health Information Center (SHIC), Equine Disease Communication Center (US Equestrian), USDA APHIS / NAHLN and Texas Animal Health Commission (mandatory reporting). White space: Verdict basis: I found no commercial or non-commercial system that turns weekly counts from US large-animal (cattle) vet practices into a regional syndromic index sold to institutional buyers. I could not test that claim against Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch or Product Hunt, so treat it as unconfirmed on the startup side.

What exists today:
- Academic systems, mostly in Europe (SAVSNET/FAVSNET in the UK).
- A 2025 scoping review of 126 animal syndromic systems: 67 percent were still proof-of-concept, only 20 percent were fully operational, and it noted that even established systems are vulnerable to loss of funding. Operational ones were mostly government run. This is a nearby-review finding, not proof that nobody is building this in the US. Source: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40327964
- Free industry models such as MSHMP (swine) and the equine EDCC.
- Companion-animal practice data businesses (Animalytix, Vetsource).
- Government mandatory reporting, which now covers confirmed and suspected screwworm within 24 hours in Texas.

Unserved, specifically:
1. Pre-confirmation, syndromic, cattle-specific signals: abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and milk drops, at ZIP3 or county level, weekly. Government reporting only covers confirmed or suspected reportable disease.
2. A denominator and absence-of-calls signal that no current system produces.
3. A decision-grade product for private actors who face NWS movement restrictions and have no ground-level feed: sale barns, order buyers, feedlots, packers, insurers and animal health territory teams.

Structural risks that keep this a gap rather than open:
- Government and free alternatives (TAHC and USDA public case counts, EDCC-style free alerts) satisfy much of the need.
- Vets are legally obligated to report suspects to TAHC, so a private feed adds little for confirmed cases.
- Privacy and trade-implication concerns were the top barrier in an Australian stakeholder study (https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40037116).
- Selling vet-sourced early disease signals to commodity funds carries legal and ethics exposure (material non-public information, duty-to-report conflicts).

title: Mzee's Testament: Family Land Councils Before Death
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of untangling the dead man's land after the funeral, hold a video-witnessed Family Land Council this December while the parent is alive and every heir is home, lock it into a will, family agreement, capacity certificate and time-locked vault, and grow the format into a registry of family land intent.
customer: Diaspora and urban children (30-55) with living rural parents aged 65-90 who hold unsubdivided family land. The child pays in September-November for a December council, but the parent is the legal client of the partner advocate. Later payers are SACCOs, lenders and insurers who buy verified family land plans (with family consent), and churches and clan associations as channels.
problem: After death, succession takes 1-3 years, is contested and costs heirs dearly (parent's figures). Every year of delay means heirs die, feuds harden, and evidence disappears. Children abroad only get all siblings into one compound at Christmas. Parents avoid 'death talk' and fear that gifting land makes them dependants. Where informal wills exist they are often unwitnessed or challenged for lack of capacity or undue influence, and daughters and second households are frequently excluded by custom, which produces litigation later. No one sells a cheap, provable record of what the parent actually wanted, agreed by all children while the parent can still speak.
solution: 'Family Land Council': a one-day facilitated event at the family home in the 20 Dec to 5 Jan window, prepared in October-November by WhatsApp intake, an official title search, a heir list including second households and a parcel sketch. On the day a team of three attends: a facilitator, a partner advocate who acts for the parent and first meets the parent alone, and a videographer, plus a clinician's capacity assessment on site or the same week. Outputs: (1) the parent's recorded, parent-alone statement of wishes; (2) a Family Land Agreement signed by all adult children in person or by video (allocation, parent's lifetime use and residence, burial ground, provision for daughters and widows); (3) a properly witnessed will drafted by the advocate; (4) an encrypted Family Land Vault holding video, documents and a machine-readable Family Land Plan, released to named heirs only when a death certificate is uploaded and two heirs confirm. Optional track: transfer by gift or subdivision with the parent's use protected, through surveyor, Land Control Board consent and registry, which skips the court queue entirely. The exact legal structure (gift versus will, consent requirements, stamp duty treatment) must be confirmed with Kenyan counsel.
why_now: December 2026 is about ten weeks away and diaspora flights are booked in October-November, so the product's launch window is literal. The allottee generation is 65-90 now: each year removes some of the people whose testimony is the whole point. LLMs, phone video and e-signature make an evidence pack cheap, and drafting is commoditising (Wakili-Intel, July 2026) while witnessing, capacity evidence and convening a family are not. Remittances of roughly US$5bn a year (parent's figure, verify) show families already pay to 'sort out the land' from abroad. This would have worked in 2019 only as a boutique law-firm service; the cost of running councils at scale with intake, video and vault software is new.
revenue_model: Council package: KES 40k service fee (about US$310) for pre-work, facilitation, video and capacity evidence and vault setup, pilot price KES 25k. The advocate's will and agreement drafting (KES 15-25k, assumption) is billed directly by the advocate to the parent as client, and the clinician's fee is passed through at cost. Vault subscription KES 3k a year per family (annual refresh video on the parent's birthday, updates for births, marriages and deaths), target 60% attach. Gift or subdivision track: KES 20k service fee on top of surveyor, Land Control Board and registry costs at cost. Later B2B: per-verified-plan fees from SACCOs, lenders and insurers, with consent. Year one aim: 50-60 councils, about KES 2M revenue at roughly 55% gross margin (cost about KES 14-18k per council), validating the model rather than making money. Scale-up: church and clan chapters delivering 500+ councils per December.
non_obvious_insight: The paying child is the likeliest future litigant, so the product only works if the parent is the client: parent alone on tape, an independent advocate, a capacity certificate and a cooling-off period. That evidence can only be produced while the parent is alive, which is why no post-death service, however good, can replace it. December is the one moment all 8-20 heirs are physically together and emotionally invested, so the coordination problem that costs a year after death costs a day before it. The inversion also turns a one-off dead-paperwork job into a living, recurring relationship (vault refresh, births and deaths) whose data compounds into a standard-setting registry of family land intent.
first_30_days: October: recruit two advocates who do wills and agree a parent-as-client engagement letter, and one clinician for capacity assessments. Run a dry-run council for a friendly family (Murang'a or Kakamega) to time the day and script the parent-alone interview. Launch a landing page and WhatsApp booking with 30 December slots at the KES 25k pilot price and a 30% M-Pesa deposit, sold through diaspora Facebook and WhatsApp groups, church and alumni networks, with a free 'Family Land Map' quiz as lead magnet. Recruit and train four facilitators (paralegals, community mobilisers, retired chief's assistants). Targets: 15 paid slots by 30 October and 30 by end of November. The riskiest assumption is that parents agree, so measure the parent-consent rate among families whose child pays (target above 60%).

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Luru (open-source 'Kenya's Digital Succession Copilot'), Wakili-Intel (AI drafting copilot for Kenyan advocates), Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority (UFAA), Ardhisasa (Ministry of Lands digital land registry). White space: Provisional, because the web search budget hit its 200-call cap before any search returned results. My evidence comes only from direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches. I found no funded startup, product or open-source project that combines (a) diaspora-paid flat-fee intake, (b) heir mapping across Kenyan name variants, (c) field-agent collection of chief's letters and thumbprint or video consent from 8-20 relatives, and (d) hand-off to partner advocates. The software pieces (family tree, readiness score, drafting copilots) exist only as zero-star hobby repos. Government platforms (Ardhisasa, court e-filing, UFAA) cover filing and claiming but not multi-heir coordination. UFAA's beneficiary claim rule makes succession a prerequisite for claiming a dead person's unclaimed assets, so a succession-first product that unlocks those assets has a logical hook. The unserved wedge is the coordination and evidence-gathering layer sold to the paying sibling abroad. Luru scores post-death readiness and Wakili-Intel drafts pleadings for advocates, both software, both after death, neither with field or convening capability. UFAA is a post-death channel; Ardhisasa and court e-filing are bypassed on the gift track and used on the succession track. Incumbents do not respond because advocates earn more from contested post-death matters and courts, the Public Trustee and funeral insurers do not run family meetings. The main threat is a government wills registry, which the format, vault and process still complement. Defensibility: data on family plans accepted by chiefs, SACCOs and lenders (network economies, cornered resource) and process power in running parent-safe councils.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing
one_liner: A continuous, coder-signed check on whether ambient AI scribe notes actually support the E/M levels being billed, before the payers or the government find out.
customer: Compliance officers, CFOs and revenue-integrity leaders at health systems and physician groups (20-500 providers), MSOs and PE-backed groups that rolled out ambient AI scribes. Secondary buyer: acquirers doing diligence on scribe-enabled practices.
problem: After ambient scribe rollouts, E/M distributions shift toward 99204-5 and 99214-5. Studies of six health systems show high-acuity visit share up roughly 12-20 points for new visits. Payers respond with AI downcoding and record requests, and the False Claims Act exposure is real if notes carry exam elements or time statements that did not happen. The scribe vendor cannot credibly audit itself, and annual compliance audits of 5-10 charts per provider cannot see systemic drift.
solution: Step 1 is a claims-only drift diagnostic (no EHR integration): compare each provider's E/M and modifier distribution before and after go-live with specialty benchmarks and peers, and rank the provider outliers. Step 2 is a targeted sample review by certified coders of the flagged encounters, checking that MDM or total-time really support the level. Copied-forward text, unsupported time attestations and orders without documented reasoning are the failure patterns. Step 3 is a continuing dashboard plus quarterly audit memos designed to be shown to a payer, auditor or the OIG. It includes a payer downcoding forecast.
why_now: Ambient scribes went mainstream across health systems in 2025-26. Research is documenting the coding-intensity increase and describing a payer-provider 'coding arms race', and payers are turning to their own AI for downcoding. The OIG's compliance program guidance expects organizations to audit new technology used in billing. Nobody independent has a standard offering yet.
revenue_model: $8-15 per audited encounter, or $15-30 per provider per month for the drift monitor plus sampled audits. Enterprise annual contracts of $50-200k. Diligence engagements at $10-25k each.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not template bloat that scribes create in the HPI and exam. Under the 2021 E/M rules those elements do not count toward the level. The risk is that the scribe's fluent narration makes medical decision making and time statements sound stronger than what the physician did, and audits succeed or fail on MDM and time. Only coders who have survived payer audits know this. That is why a coder-signed audit is worth more than a model score, and why a compliance officer needs a third party, not the scribe vendor's coding module.
first_30_days: Find 3 mid-size groups, ideally with 30-100 providers, that adopted a scribe in the last 12 months, through LinkedIn outreach to compliance and revenue-integrity leads. Offer a free claims-only drift diagnostic, since 12 months of CPT data from their billing system is enough. Show them the outlier providers. Convert to a paid sample-audit engagement ($10-25k) and a monthly monitor. Recruit two certified auditors (CPC, CPMA) as contractors.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface.

title: Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator
one_liner: An advice-only LINE tool that tells franchise convenience-store owners how many fresh items to order and when to mark them down, using the owner's own payoff instead of HQ's.
customer: Franchise convenience-store owners in Japan, especially the many multi-store owners (roughly 55,000 stores nationally, all three chains). They pay a monthly fee plus a share of the waste they cut. First targets are Osaka owners reachable through the franchisee union and owner LINE groups.
problem: The royalty is charged on gross profit calculated as if discarded food never existed. At Seven, HQ absorbs only 15% of disposal cost and the owner absorbs 85%. So HQ's ordering AI and the field counselors (OFC) push order quantities toward what maximizes HQ's royalty, not the owner's take-home. Take a rice ball that costs ¥100 and sells at ¥160. With a 60% royalty on the ¥60 gross profit, the owner keeps about ¥24 when it sells and loses about ¥85 when it is binned. HQ makes about ¥36 on a sale and loses about ¥15 on a discard. The owner-optimal stocking level is far lower than HQ's, and no owner has a tool that shows this. Markdowns would close much of the gap, but staff are reluctant to apply stickers and owners fear the OFC's disapproval.
solution: The owner photographs the daily disposal-scan printout and the hourly sales sheet, or forwards a CSV. The tool never touches HQ systems. Each afternoon it returns a per-category order guide such as 'cut salmon onigiri by 4 at the 16:00 delivery, add 2 tempura udon'. It also gives a markdown clock, for example 'sticker at 20:40, deeper cut at 23:10', calculated from the owner's actual royalty tier, disposal share and sell-through curve. A one-page 'why I ordered less' printout gives the owner data to answer the OFC. Phase two adds an owner-side dashboard showing true hourly wage after royalty and self-labor. It also adds a contract-exit and renegotiation calculator, and anonymized peer benchmarks that owners can use collectively.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises to ¥1,231 on 1 October 2026, up ¥54 after ¥63 last year. Labor is the biggest cost, and waste is the last controllable line item. HQ-side AI ordering is now the default, so owners increasingly follow machine suggestions they cannot audit. Chains have grudgingly allowed markdowns since the JFTC's 2009 order against Seven-Eleven Japan for obstructing them, but owners still lack tools to price them properly.
revenue_model: ¥4,900 per store per month, plus 20-25% of documented waste reduction for the first 12 months. If a store saves ¥80-100k a month, the fee is easy to justify. Multi-store owners get a bundle. Later revenue comes from an owner-benchmark subscription and referrals to specialist franchise lawyers and accountants.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is not a shared problem between HQ and owner. The contract makes it the owner's problem alone, while HQ's revenue is almost indifferent to it. The newsvendor critical ratio for the owner is about 22%, versus about 70% for HQ. Every 'AI ordering recommendation' is optimized for the wrong party's payoff. Nobody built the owner's-side calculator because owners fear retaliation and VCs assume HQ systems are neutral.
first_30_days: Use my three stores as the lab. Photograph two weeks of disposal sheets and hourly sales, then back-test the newsvendor plus markdown model against what actually happened. Build a LINE bot with photo OCR and a spreadsheet engine. Recruit 10 owners from union chat groups and Facebook franchisee groups. Run a free 4-week gain-share pilot with a signed baseline for each store. Publish a one-page 'royalty asymmetry' explainer that spreads owner-to-owner. Convert the pilot to paid at week 5.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified.

title: Family Bank: Bank of Mom and Dad, Papered
one_liner: A family office's real job is governance and records, not investing; for $20/mo, give ordinary parents and adult children a promissory-note, autopay and sibling-fairness ledger for the money that already flows between them.
customer: Parents aged 55-75 who lend or give money to adult children (down-payment help, car, tuition, debt payoff, business start), sold as a pair with the adult child (28-45). Elder-law attorneys, mortgage brokers and credit unions are referral channels.
problem: Family lending is handshake-based. Zero-interest loans over $10k invite imputed-interest questions. Gifts above the $19,000 annual exclusion (2026) need Form 709 filings. Medicaid's 60-month look-back treats gifts and forgiven loans as transfers. Mortgage lenders want documented gift letters. Siblings fight at inheritance over who got what because nobody kept records. NAR's 2025 profile shows the median first-time buyer is 40 and 22% received a gift or loan from relatives or friends.
solution: A guided flow decides gift vs loan and generates a note at or above the AFR (August 2026: 4.10% short, 4.35% mid, 4.92% long). ACH autopay collects and pays, and both sides get annual interest statements. A December 'forgiveness engine' forgives up to the exclusion with proper letters. A sibling ledger records every advancement so estates can equalize. Flags fire for Form 709 and Medicaid look-back exposure, and there is a mortgage-ready gift-letter generator plus one-click export to the family's estate attorney. Attorney review is an add-on.
why_now: Median first-time buyer age hit 40 (a record), housing costs push more family help, and long-term-care costs make the Medicaid look-back a live worry for boomer parents. Instant-payment and bank-linking rails make autopay cheap. The 2026 federal estate exemption is $15M, so for most families the value is peace and records, not tax planning.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family (up to 3 active loans); $49 document packs for the free-to-paid funnel; $149 attorney review add-on with referral fees; optional servicing fee; later, a pooled family reserve product.
non_obvious_insight: The killer feature is not the loan, it is the sibling ledger. Most family money fights are about unequal treatment nobody can prove, and family offices solve this with an advancement ledger that ordinary families never get. The loan-vs-gift label is also the pivot point for tax and Medicaid consequences, so classification is the paid moment.
first_30_days: Ship a free AFR calculator and note generator aimed at 'family loan agreement' searches, and sell $49 document packs. Convert 5% to the $20/mo servicing tier. Line up 3 elder-law attorneys who receive leads and review notes. Target 50 paying families.
