title: Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel
one_liner: Turn the ~55 GW of idle data center backup generators into dispatchable capacity by solving the air-permit problem instead of the hardware problem.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets. Secondary buyers are utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Data centers hold about 55 GW of backup diesel (Virginia alone has about 27 GW permitted), and it runs 10-30 minutes a month. PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring their own capacity or be curtailed. Air permits cap non-emergency run hours, so nobody can legally count these engines as capacity.
solution: Fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' packages. They cover a state-specific permit modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits), engineering and financing for emissions retrofits on the subset of engines that need them, and paralleling/telemetry upgrades. Enrollment in PJM's on-site backup (IRAS-style) and demand-response programs comes with third-party measurement and verification. Runtime is capped at a few dozen to ~100 hours a year, dispatched only in system emergencies, with community disclosure built in.
why_now: PJM's July auction shortfall, the proposed backstop auction (15-year terms, $555/MW-day cap) and the curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule make backup generation valuable for the first time. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so this fleet is the only large block of capacity that exists today.
revenue_model: $40-150k fixed fee per site for permit and engineering work, plus 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the $325/MW-day cap a 20 MW fleet is worth very roughly $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fee is easy to justify. Retrofit financing adds a spread.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest big block of new PJM capacity is not new. It is already built and sitting behind a fence, and the barrier is air-permit lawyering that VC-backed hardware companies ignore. A repeatable per-state permit playbook is the moat. Emergency-only runtime is why it works: at under 1% of hours, the capacity value dwarfs the emissions.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permit files for ~30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL. Build a 'permit headroom map' showing run-hour caps and engine tiers. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit of a 20+ MW fleet and aim to close two paid pilots.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead.

title: Shared-Aide Pods for 55+ Apartment Buildings
one_liner: One on-site aide team serves 6-10 residents in the same building, delivering assisted-living-style help at a fraction of 1:1 home-care cost.
customer: Owners and operators of independent-living and 55+ apartment buildings (market-rate, senior LIHTC and HUD-202 properties). The payers are middle-income residents and their families, who can't afford $75-130k a year and are stuck on waitlists.
problem: Home care is sold as one aide per client per hour ($35 an hour, about $80k a year for 44 hours a week) only because of legacy billing. Assisted living is at 90% occupancy with almost no new supply before 2030. Residents who age past independent living either move out or go without.
solution: A licensed home-care agency subsidiary (or partnership with one) posts 2-3 aides per shift inside the building. They run scheduled 15-45 minute ADL, medication-reminder, meal-setup and toileting visits, plus overnight response. Dispatch software handles acuity tiers and in-building routing (floors, elevators). Residents buy monthly tiers of about $1,800-3,500, and the property gets a retention amenity.
why_now: NIC MAP shows 57 of 99 metros above 90% occupancy, units under construction at a 2012 low, and no meaningful new supply before 2030. Medicaid HCBS is walled off by 15-month waitlists and labor is scarcer after the 2026 visa pause, so stretching each aide across more clients is the only lever left.
revenue_model: Monthly resident subscription by care tier, with a revenue share or amenity fee to the property owner. Later, Medicaid HCBS or managed-care billing for pods in affordable senior buildings.
non_obvious_insight: Aide hours are cheap to make dense (no drive time, no client-hour minimums) but are priced as if they were mobile. The gap between 1:1 pricing and 1:8 cost is the whole business, and only a property-anchored operator can capture it. Assisted-living-without-the-license is a real category nobody has scaled.
first_30_days: Sign a 90-day pilot with one 100-200 unit 55+ property in a tight market. Subcontract to an existing licensed agency to move quickly, staff a two-aide pod, and target 15 residents at about $2,200 a month. Track aide minutes per resident and move-out avoidance.

Serious risks that shrink the white space:
- Licensing. Under Minnesota 144G.08, sleeping accommodations plus any 'assisted living services' (personal care, toileting help, medication reminders, meal setup, safety checks) under contract requires an assisted-living license. Subsidized housing is excluded unless marketed as assisted living, and the statute does not address a property owner that arranges a home-care provider on site. 'Assisted-living-without-the-license' is therefore legally fragile in many states, especially with an owner revenue share and overnight response, which look like 'holding out'.
- Unit economics. Two aides per shift is 17,520 aide-hours a year, about $400-500k loaded at roughly $23-28 an hour. Spread over 15 residents at $2,200 a month ($396k a year) that is break-even at best. At 6-10 residents the cost per resident is about $4,000-5,000 a month, which is above the stated $1,800-3,500 tiers. The idea's own numbers are internally inconsistent (6-10 residents in the one-liner, 15 in the pilot).
- Substitutes. BAYADA and franchise agencies already market to senior-living partners, and NCR and Brookdale could add pods in-house.

title: Work-Permit Gap Desk for Frontline Employers
one_liner: Employer-paid, pre-cliff delay suits for workers whose EAD renewals are pending, sold to home-care, nursing and staffing employers as a per-worker maintenance plan instead of a one-off legal purchase.
customer: HR and compliance directors or owners of 150-1,500 employee home-care agencies, skilled-nursing operators and staffing firms in the NYC-metro and New Jersey area (workers resident in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J., where delay suits most often end in agency action), each with hundreds of workers on time-limited work authorization (asylum-pending, adjustment-pending, parole and DACA categories). The worker is the lawyer's client; the employer is the payer and the buyer of the platform. Later channel: I-9/E-Verify vendors, PEOs and state home-care and staffing associations.
problem: Employers eat the cliff. Since the 540-day automatic EAD extension ended for renewals filed from late Oct 2025, a worker whose I-765 renewal is still pending on the expiry date must come off the schedule. A care agency watches a predictable slice of its workforce disappear for months, pays replacement and onboarding costs, and has no lever to pull. Its HR team already tracks every expiry date for I-9 compliance, but that process ends at 'alert' with no remedy step. Immigration counsel are hired by individuals or for petitions like H-1B and PERM, never as an operations service for frontline workforces, so this problem has no owner.
solution: Gap Desk in three parts. (1) Free EAD Gap Calculator: HR uploads employee ID, EAD category code and expiry date (no names), and gets the projected number of workers who will hit expiry before a decision, priced in lost margin and replacement cost. (2) Enrolled program: the employer offers a voluntary benefit to every employee with time-limited work authorization regardless of nationality (to limit anti-discrimination exposure). The platform watches filing date against expiry; when a ledger-set trigger fires (case beyond posted time and expiry approaching), it obtains the worker's consent and files through a panel of federal-admitted attorneys at a flat fee. Structure: the worker is the client, the employer pays as a third-party payer with informed consent (independent judgment and confidentiality preserved), and the employer sees only a status date. (3) Bridge kit: job-hold and leave templates and a reinstatement re-verification checklist so the employer keeps the seat during the gap. Out of scope by design: TPS terminations, revoked parole and denials, which are not delay problems.
why_now: The auto-extension ended in Oct 2025, and Mandamus.com's case-law tracker calls I-765 mandamus a 'primary remedy' since then, so the cliff is new and the remedy is proven. Expiry dates are known 6-12 months ahead, so the risk is forecastable. Care-sector labor is scarce, making each lost seat expensive. LLM drafting plus a per-district ledger lets a panel attorney turn a routine I-765 suit in about an hour, making a $1,750 flat fee profitable. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern matches the length of a typical gap.
revenue_model: Employer pays $5 per covered worker per month (monitoring, calculator, case management) plus $2,000 per triggered case: $1,750 paid directly to the panel attorney and $250 to the platform as a flat administrative fee. Never a percentage of the legal fee. Illustration for a 400-worker agency: $24k/year subscription plus about 20 triggered cases (about $5k platform, $35k to attorneys). Assumption to validate in pilots: a 90-day gap costs an agency roughly $5-10k in lost margin and replacement, so 20 avoided gaps clearly exceed the roughly $59k program cost. Year 2: I-9 vendors and PEOs resell for a cut of the subscription only.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the most to lose from a stuck case is the employer, yet employers have never been the buyer because immigration law treats the individual as the client; third-party payer rules allow the employer to pay while the worker stays the client. Once the employer pays, the product changes character: expiry dates are known a year ahead, so demand is a forecastable renewal calendar and recurring subscription instead of lumpy, panicked legal purchases. And the employer's I-9 tickler is already the distribution asset, since it holds exactly the dates that trigger the suit.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the calculator as a spreadsheet plus web form and run it on anonymized expiry lists from 3 friendly employers. Days 1-10: sign 2-3 panel attorneys admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J. at $1,750 flat and get an employment-law read on third-party-payer, anti-discrimination and prepaid-legal-plan rules. Days 7-30: contact about 60 NYC-metro and NJ home-care agencies and staffing firms through state association events and LinkedIn, lead with their own calculator output, and close 3 paid pilots at about $2,500/month concierge plus per-case fees. Go/no-go: at least one employer with a real expiring cohort authorizes a filing within 30 days, and outcomes are logged to seed the ledger.
lineage: mutation of I1062 ('Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats. | How this version avoids them: Mandamus.com sells single suits to individuals at $5,000 with SEO funnels and cannot run a workforce calendar for an employer. I-9/E-Verify vendors track expiry dates but stop at an alert (not verified in this research); they are channel partners, not rivals. Docketwise and Boundless serve firms and individuals on petitions, not employer-paid remedies. Alma sells O-1/EB-1 strategy to companies for high-skill hires, not frontline EAD renewals. Large corporate immigration firms serve professionals where ticket sizes are big; a $1,750 frontline case is below their radar (unverified). DoNotPay and free pro se guides cannot give an employer a managed, attorney-signed service with status reporting. Employer ownership of the buyer relationship is the wedge none of them hold.

title: Paid-But-Dark: Solar Loan Book Audit
one_liner: A fixed-fee audit and ongoing watch that tells credit unions, servicers and ABS holders which of their solar loans finance a roof that was never switched on. It then cures the worst ones through a supplier-neutral contractor bench.
customer: Wedge: chief credit or risk officers and loss-mitigation heads at mid-size credit unions and community banks that hold indirect solar loans originated through installer dealer networks. Second wave: servicers and ABS controlling-class investors that inherited books from failed platforms (Solar Servicing LLC-type). Deliberately not the seven Freedom Forever financiers, who already have ops teams and are already staffed. Start with legacy books from Titan, SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, and Mosaic- and Sunlight-financed loans.
problem: Loan tapes track payments, not power. Many dealer-channel programs released milestone money at 'installed', so a loan on a dark roof looks like ordinary credit stress and gets routed to collections, which is the wrong workout. The holder cannot tell installer-caused non-payment from real credit distress. Reserves are mis-sized and nobody in the institution owns the question 'is the system switched on?'. Judges flagged three weaknesses in the parent: the first wave is already staffed, paperwork-only jobs are price-pressured (Atma quotes up to about $1,200), and demand is lumpy.
solution: Step 1, a 10-day Book Audit. Ingest the loan tape (address, funding dates, installer ID, milestone dates). Cross-match it to county permit portals, public state interconnection datasets, borrower-authorized monitoring links and installer status. Output a loan-level tier: Energized, Dark-fixable, Dark-blocked-by-records, or Never-started. Add cost-to-cure, expected recovered loan value, and a one-page loss-reserve summary the CFO can hand to auditors. Step 2, a quarterly PTO-lag surveillance subscription on the whole book and on new originations, with installer-health flags, so nothing goes dark silently again. Step 3, cure orchestration at fixed prices by tier, using an open bench (Atma-type installers, Revival, ECG, Optimus, laid-off crews) and engineering subs. GreenLancer can be a supplier here. The paperwork-only tier is passed through at roughly the $1.2k benchmark plus a fixed coordination fee. The margin lives in the audit, the surveillance and the hard tiers (missing hardware, inspection fixes).
why_now: Freedom Forever went to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026 (claims due Oct 16). It showed that lenders could not see which loans sat on dark roofs, and the same problem is buried in older Titan, SunPower, Sunnova and PosiGen books. The 25D credit ended for 2026 expenditures, so origination volume is down and more installer failures are likely. First-principles cost stack: reading messy permit files and utility portals used to cost $100+ of coordinator time per job. Document and browser agents now do it for a few dollars, so a per-loan audit can be priced below a credit union's discretionary-spend threshold at good margin.
revenue_model: Audit at $10-20 per loan with a $30k minimum (a 3,000-loan book is about $45-60k). Surveillance at $3-6 per loan per year. Cure coordination fee of $300 on paperwork-only jobs. A 20-30% markup on hard-tier cures ($3-8k each). A $500 PTO bonus. Later, licensing of per-AHJ and per-utility playbooks. Bottom-up: 60 institutions in 24 months at about $60k first-year value is about $3.6M before any cure revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The lender's blind spot is a missing column, not missing crews. Selling to the CFO or CRO's loss-reserve problem, instead of to a loss-mitigation desk waiting for the next bankruptcy, turns event-driven demand into continuous demand. Because the audit is a small fixed-fee purchase and not a vendor selection, it slips under procurement thresholds and creates its own list of jobs to cure. A finding of 'this roof is dark' changes the workout from collections to cure, which is where the loan value is recovered.
first_30_days: Week 1: hold 5 calls with credit union CROs and servicer COOs. Ask what they pay today, whether GreenLancer or anyone already covers them, and who owns the reserve question. This is the kill test: if GreenLancer's seven financiers already cover servicers and credit unions, downgrade. Weeks 1-3: build the screen on public data for one state that publishes interconnection records (California's DG Stats is the largest). Publish an anonymized ZIP-level 'permit-final-but-no-PTO' index for Titan and Freedom Forever-era permits as a lead magnet, with no homeowner addresses. Weeks 2-4: offer 3 credit unions a free NDA'd 300-loan scan with a paid full-book option. Recruit 2 ex-installer permit coordinators and sign 2 licensed subs. Goal: one signed paid audit within 60 days.

This sells book-level visibility to holders that have no ops, owns the data layer GreenLancer lacks, and buys GreenLancer-style engineering as a supplier. The seven named lenders and Sunrun/GoodLeap crews keep their in-house step-in, and we do not chase them. We target credit unions, servicers, ABS holders and legacy books. Atma, Revival, ECG and Optimus are the labor bench and not rivals. OhmSnap is homeowner lead-gen and Solar Insure sells warranties to owners after the fact. Enphase's program is post-PTO upsell. title: Revenue-Integrity Diligence for Water System Acquirers
one_liner: The buyer of a small or mid-size water system pays for a 10-day, account-level scan of the target's billing, meters and parcels. It prices hidden revenue and revenue-quality risk before signing, then a success fee on prospectively recovered revenue funds the first-100-days fix.
customer: Corporate development and integration leads at serial acquirers of municipal and small private water and wastewater systems. These are the acquisition teams of investor-owned utilities, PE- and infrastructure-fund-backed water platforms, contract operators bidding O&M or concession deals with revenue share, and regional authorities absorbing failing systems. Deal size is systems with 3k-60k connections.
problem: Buyers price municipal systems on reported revenue and customer counts. Their diligence covers engineering condition, financial audit and legal. Nobody tests account-level billing integrity beyond sampling a few bills. Sellers cannot fix leakage themselves: correcting a meter class, adding unbilled connections or raising a billing floor is politically radioactive for a council, and back-billing is legally capped. So the leakage stays buried until after close. The buyer then discovers it over years, after the price is set, so the buyer neither benefits from knowing it at pricing time nor budgets capex against it. The same blind spot hides negative surprises: estimated reads, stopped meters, dead accounts and customer counts that overstate the base.
solution: Ask the seller's data room for a standard extract: account list, 24-36 months of consumption, meter inventory, rate class and tariff, receivables aging. Join it to the assessor roll, building footprints, permits and public filings. Produce a Revenue Integrity Report in 10 days: (1) a parcels-with-structures versus billed-connections gap by service area; (2) a large-meter low-flow fingerprint ranking accounts by expected annual dollars; (3) read-quality and zero-read audit (estimated reads, stopped meters); (4) misclassified rate class or meter size; (5) a downside adjustment to the revenue baseline; (6) a 100-day plan with a prospective-only fix, a meter test and replacement list, and a price-adjustment memo for negotiations. After close, execute the plan with the buyer's CIS and the field-test subcontractor, and later normalize billing data across the buyer's whole portfolio.
why_now: PFAS, lead-line and aging-pipe capex plus affordability politics push small municipal owners toward selling or regionalizing. Serial acquirers and infrastructure funds are actively rolling up water systems. Fair-market-value sale statutes (for example Pennsylvania's Act 12) have made municipal sales a repeatable process. Diligence windows are short (30-60 days of exclusivity), which fits a 10-day data product. Open footprint data, interval data and LLM-assisted cleaning of messy municipal billing exports make a 10-day turnaround possible for two people.
revenue_model: Fixed diligence fee of $35-75k per target, paid from the deal budget and owed even if the buyer walks. Success fee of 15-20% of verified incremental billed revenue over 24 months post-close (prospective only, verifiable in the buyer's own CIS). Optional 100-day revenue plan retainer of $15k a month. Then a portfolio SaaS tier for serial acquirers: $3-6k per system per year for cross-system revenue-integrity monitoring. Bottom-up assumption: 30-60 diligence engagements a year at about $50k is $1.5-3M of revenue for a small team.
non_obvious_insight: The same $1 of recurring recovered revenue is worth about $1 a year in a city budget, but roughly 8-15x that to an acquirer valuing the system on earnings, and the buyer can bill correctly on day one. Change of ownership is the only moment when meter-class and connection corrections carry no council optics and no back-billing exposure. Payer and problem-owner are misaligned in the parent idea (the city pays for a fight it does not want). Moving the buyer of the utility into the payer seat removes procurement, contingency-ban and optics risk in one step. It also works as an option-free downside screen, which a buyer values on every deal, not only the rich ones.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 40 acquirers from state PUC acquisition dockets, fair-market-value sale filings and municipal sale RFPs. Pick three live or recently announced sale processes. Run a free public-data teaser for each: assessor parcels with structures inside the service area versus service connections in SDWIS and PUC filings, plus the top customers in the seller's annual financial report. Send two-page teasers to corporate development heads. Recruit one advisor, either ex-corporate development at a water utility platform or a water-M&A deal lawyer, for warm intros. Offer a half-price pilot diligence ($15-20k) on one live deal with a data-room extract. Confirm buyers' NDAs allow use of aggregated, anonymized yield data.
lineage: mutation of I0388 ('Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Itron (Temetra Analysis / Non-Revenue Water portfolio), Badger Meter (BEACON, OneNetwork), Master Meter (Harmony Encore MDM), Metron-Farnier (WaterScope). White space: Important caveat: my WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran. This verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches, not on broad web, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweeps. Treat 'no direct competitor found' as unconfirmed, and do a manual pass on Crunchbase, YC and RFP portals before committing. What I did verify: (1) I found no vendor selling a contingency-fee service that joins assessor roll, footprints, imagery and the billing system to produce named unbilled addresses for water utilities. (2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. (3) The GitHub search for open-source tools found nothing relevant. Genuinely unserved: an independent, outcome-priced screen of large-account meter accuracy that ranks specific accounts by expected dollars using consumption history, and that does not depend on one meter vendor's hardware. Ghost-parcel discovery is the weaker half. A structure with no account is rare where permits trigger taps, and an ADU on a shared meter is usually already billed on consumption. Back-billing is politically and legally messy, and some jurisdictions restrict contingency contracts. The larger risk is structural (yield, procurement law, optics), not competitive. | How this version avoids them: Itron, Badger, Master Meter and Metron sell hardware plus analytics to utilities that already own the system, and they do nothing at deal time. Ameresco-style ESCOs sell projects after ownership is settled. Rate and valuation consultancies (Raftelis, FCS, Hazen and peers) are often on the seller side or the municipality's side, and they use sampled tests rather than account-level joins, which makes a buyer-side, conflict-free diligence product counter-positioned against them. Big-4 and engineering diligence cover financial and asset condition, not billing integrity. The AWWA audit is system-level and free but names no accounts. EagleView and BlueConduit sell parcel data or a lead inventory, not a buyer-paid revenue-quality report. There is no public procurement and no contingency-contract exposure, because the payer is a private acquirer.

title: Ship-Date Cliff Audits for Phased Campuses
one_liner: A fixed-fee clock-map, rider-negotiation and proof-test sprint for developers of multi-phase data center campuses whose pre-bought gensets, UPS and chillers were shipped long before the halls they serve, so the OEM 18-months-from-ship outer limit expires before startup.
customer: Wedge buyer: the VP of procurement or construction director at colo developers and neoclouds building multi-phase campuses (100MW+, with phases 2-4 not yet energized) that accepted long-lead MEP deliveries ahead of the shell. Start with generators, then UPS. Secondary buyer: the lender's technical advisor asking for an equipment warranty schedule at draw or refinancing.
problem: The judges and the competitor check both found that the parent's premise is too broad. Startup plus load-bank IST already loads most equipment, so the 'idle hall' exposure is narrow. The clean exposure is different. OEM terms run to the earlier of about 12 months from startup or 18 months from factory ship (Cummins, Eaton and Trane terms in the research). Developers buy gear in blocks for phases 2-4 to lock lead-time slots and pre-tariff prices, and take delivery into yards or spare rooms. When a phase slips, the outer limit lapses before the unit is ever started. Storage voiding conditions (heaters, battery freshening charges, engine exercise) are usually undocumented, so an OEM can also deny on those grounds. Procurement has moved on, the ship date lives in a bill of lading nobody rereads, and ops inherits the unit with no idea the clock ran out.
solution: 1) Cliff calendar. Per serial number, extract ship date (bill of lading, delivery ticket), planned startup, outer-limit date and voiding conditions. The LLM pipeline is an internal tool; the deliverable is a one-page dated list of cliffs. 2) Rider sprint. Before each cliff, negotiate a written start-date deferral or delayed-start rider with the OEM. Package it campus-wide, because the owner's phase 3-4 orders are the leverage a single-unit rider buyer lacks. 3) Storage-compliance repair. Fix missing exercise, heater and battery-charge logs so the OEM loses its easy denial grounds. 4) Proof test. For installed units 6-9 months before the cliff, run a staged load test using a load-bank rental partner, then file claims with OEM-grade evidence while the OEM is still liable. Contingency is not the lead model.
why_now: Long-lead power gear (gensets, transformers, switchgear) is being bought years ahead of buildings, and phase slippage is widespread in 2026 reporting. Tariffs make each unit more expensive, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs make serial-level extraction from delivery documents cheap. Delayed-start riders exist (Trane), so the ask is normal to OEMs but rarely made.
revenue_model: $30-60K fixed fee per campus phase for the cliff calendar plus rider negotiation. $60-120K per year campus retainer that keeps the calendar live as phases progress. Load-test pass-through with a 15% markup, plus a referral fee from the rental partner. Success fee of 20% of OEM-accepted claim value, measured by the OEM's claim number or credit memo, and 10% of the discount won on riders versus list. Assumption to validate: about 30 campus programs at roughly $80K per year is about $2.4M ARR with 2-3 people.
non_obvious_insight: The exposed population is defined by shipment date versus startup date, not by whether a hall is idle. That makes it provable from documents and public filings before any owner talks to you. It also makes the contingency-collection problem disappear: a signed deferral or an OEM credit memo is a countable outcome, unlike 'avoided repair cost'. The leverage is future orders across the campus, which the owner has and a one-off rider purchase does not.
first_30_days: Build a target list from public state air-permit filings for backup diesel generators, which typically list unit counts and models by phase, cross-referenced with press releases and county filings. Rank 40 campuses where permitted units far exceed operating ones. Email the procurement lead a one-page teaser: 'if your gensets shipped in Q3 2025, the OEM outer limit lands in Q1 2027'. Land three owners who hand over POs and delivery tickets for a free 5-day clock map. Use the first dated cliff to open a rider conversation with the OEM before any invoice. This also answers the parent's unresolved question of whether clocks are truly running out on unstarted equipment.
lineage: mutation of I0229 ('Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline. | How this version avoids them: Ethyco and other Cx firms start their 10-month review after occupancy, so they sell to Cx and ops. This sells earlier, to procurement, and starts at shipment; it can also be white-labeled to them. Anyset, Nomic and Equipment Warranty Log commoditize extraction and stop at the ledger, so extraction is hidden here and the product is a dated outcome (signed deferral, accepted claim). Trane's delayed-start rider is a per-unit list product; a campus-wide negotiated deferral backed by future orders is not, and the rider becomes an input this business brokers. Wind, PV and BESS players (SGS, Sinovoltaics, TWAICE) serve other asset classes. CxPlanner and Bluerithm own punch lists, not shipment dates. Aggreko and Sunbelt Solomon are suppliers and referrers, not rivals. The judges' contingency-collection flaw is removed by leading with a fixed fee.

title: ERCOT Large-Load Energization Files, Fixed Fee
one_liner: A two-engineer Texas specialist that sells neocloud and colo developers a fixed-fee, six-week package of ISO-acceptable PSS/E and EMT models, a ride-through study and a compliance file, with a fee kicker paid when ERCOT accepts it.
customer: Wedge: VPs of power and interconnection leads at 30-60 mid-size neocloud, colo and AI-campus developers with 25-300 MW sites in ERCOT's large-load study queue, plus the EPCs that own their energization schedule. They have no in-house power-electronics staff. Hyperscalers with in-house power simulators are excluded on purpose.
problem: Since PGRR115 and NPRR1234 (effective late 2025), ERCOT wants studies and dynamic models for loads of 25 MW or more before energization. NOGRR282 (effective Aug 1, 2026) adds frequency and voltage ride-through requirements for large computational loads. A developer holds only OEM spec sheets. UPS and power-shelf control details sit behind OEM NDAs, and bespoke PSCAD consultants are slow and have never modeled a GPU power shelf. Every rejected model or resubmittal loop delays energization. At 100 MW of leased AI capacity, a month of slip defers roughly eight figures of rent or GPU revenue (rough estimate: about $100+/kW-month of critical IT), so a $150k package is a rounding error next to the delay it prevents.
solution:
Sell acceptance, not artifacts, in four steps.
1) A $15-25k gap analysis against the NOGRR282, PGRR115 and NPRR1234 texts, using the site's one-line diagram and UPS/PSU bill of materials.
2) A fixed-fee package of $90-180k: an ISO-submittable PSS/E dynamic model and EMT model, a ride-through and oscillation study, and a compliance file. It is built from reusable platform-level models of specific UPS, power-shelf and facility archetypes. Those models are HIL-validated at a partner lab (Typhoon HIL or OPAL-RT time, or a university lab) under OEM NDAs.
3) Submission handling and resubmittal support through ERCOT's large-load process.
4) A 25% success kicker paid on ERCOT acceptance, plus an annual re-issue subscription when GPU generation, UPS firmware or 800V DC changes the load.
why_now: NOGRR282 was approved July 9, 2026 and took effect Aug 1, 2026. PGRR115 (Nov and Dec 2025) and NPRR1234 (Dec 15, 2025) already gate energization on studies and models. The first wave of 25 MW and larger neocloud sites is hitting the queue now, before any consultancy has a large-load specialty. Rubin-generation hardware and 800V DC change the load behavior again within 12-18 months, which creates re-issue demand.
revenue_model: $15-25k gap analysis, $90-180k fixed-fee package, and a 25% success kicker on acceptance (about $25-45k). Add $20-40k per year model maintenance and re-issue per site, and later OEM test-and-listing fees for platform models. A year-1 target of about 12 packages at about $150k is roughly $1.8M with 2-3 engineers. Reuse of platform models across sites is what lifts gross margin past a consultancy's 30-40%.
non_obvious_insight: The developer does not want a model. It wants ERCOT's planners to sign off without a resubmittal loop. The durable business in inverter modeling after Blue Cut was not the model libraries, because vendors and ISOs published those. It was the shops that knew what the ISO's planners would accept. A single-regulator focus (ERCOT only) lets a two-person shop become the known acceptance expert in six months, and each accepted submission is precedent no generalist consultant has. Free generic EPRI or NERC models help us: they are conservative, and a developer who submits them risks being told to add buffer capacity or accept curtailment, while a product-specific validated model avoids that.
first_30_days: Week 1: read the actual NOGRR282 protocol text ('Large Electronic Load Ride-Through Requirements', 282NOGRR-01) and the PGRR115 and NPRR1234 submission forms. Call ERCOT large-load working group and planning contacts to confirm what compliance evidence is required. If it is self-attestation only, price down to gap analysis plus study and keep the acceptance-kicker idea for models only. Weeks 1-2: recruit one ex-ERCOT or TO planning engineer (Texas PE) and one power-electronics engineer, and publish an open ERCOT LCL Readiness Checklist. Weeks 2-4: work the public ERCOT large-load queue reports to list about 40 developers and the 10 biggest EPCs, and sell three $15k gap analyses. Sign a lab MOU and get a first UPS or power-shelf OEM NDA through the first paying customer's equipment.
lineage: mutation of I0996 ('Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Typhoon HIL (Data Centers solution), OPAL-RT (HYPERSIM, power-HIL), EPRI DCFlex, Emerald AI (Emerald Conductor). White space: Across this session's research I found no direct competitor selling packaged, hardware-validated large-load dynamic models (PSS/E plus EMT) with ride-through study reports and certification letters for GPU-cluster, PSU and UPS stacks. Nobody was seen selling OEM-level type-test certification for power shelves and UPS platforms. Adjacent players cover only pieces: HIL tools (Typhoon HIL, OPAL-RT), generic EMT consultancies, EPRI's flexibility consortium, workload-flex software (Emerald AI), and simulation software vendors with no data center library shown.

Three structural threats need answers:
1. Regulators and EPRI or NERC may publish free generic composite or EMT models, which commoditizes the model library.
2. OEMs (UPS, PSU, NVIDIA) own the confidential control details and may ship their own models.
3. Per-project EMT consulting already exists and is not verified either way for large loads.

The defensible white space is independent, hardware-validated, ISO-acceptable model packages and compliance evidence for the 25-500 MW neocloud and colo developers who lack in-house power simulators. It would be reused across sites through OEM platform type tests, not sold as bespoke studies.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before this task began, so competitor discovery relied on direct page fetches and GitHub search. Startup databases (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt), news, and NERC or EPRI publication pages were not checked. Several NERC, EPRI and PJM URLs returned 404 or empty content. Treat the 'no direct competitor' finding as moderate-confidence. Verify manually against NERC LLTF outputs, EPRI data center model reports, and WECC or ERCOT model requirements before committing. | How this version avoids them: Typhoon HIL and OPAL-RT are tool vendors, so we partner and buy their HIL time and they act as a channel. Electranix and Danovo do bespoke per-project studies for generators and transmission owners with no reusable GPU or UPS platform models and no ERCOT large-load precedent, and they are slower and costlier per site. EPRI DCFlex and free generic models are baselines we start from, not substitutes, because ERCOT wants site-specific and product-specific evidence. Emerald AI sells workload flexibility, whereas we sell compliance evidence for the fixed, fast-ramping load. Pearl Street speeds steady-state generation studies and has no dynamic large-load work. Hyperscaler in-house simulators are avoided by targeting only developers without them. Siemens PSS/E is the file format we deliver into, not a competitor.

title: Mother-Tongue Lifeline for Dementia Flashpoints
one_liner: On-demand live video calls where a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's first language and dialect coaches the English-speaking aide and calms the patient at bath, bedtime and exit-seeking moments.
customer: Home care agencies and PACE programs in immigrant-dense metros (NYC, LA, Miami, Chicago, Bay Area, Houston) with dementia clients whose aides do not share their language. Second: Medicaid managed long-term care and D-SNP plans. Third: families on a flat monthly plan.
problem: Bilingual and multilingual patients lose their second language as dementia advances and drift back to the language, dialect and idioms of their childhood. Agencies send whoever is available. The English-speaking aide cannot say the one calming phrase during the bath, so the bath fails, the patient panics, the aide gets hurt or quits, and the family blames the agency. Telephone interpretation lines translate literally, but a dementia patient's fragments and proverbs need to be validated, not translated. It is a communication problem, not an interpretation problem.
solution: A dedicated line, staffed on demand by trained bilingual retirees, nurses and teachers, covering the long tail: Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Toisanese, Cantonese, Polish, Russian, Uzbek, Punjabi, Tagalog, Greek, Armenian. A tablet or phone is propped where the patient can see it. The specialist speaks to the patient in dialect while coaching the aide in English in the earpiece: 'she's asking for her sister, say she is coming, then hum this song.' Sessions are 3-10 minutes at known flashpoints. Specialists are trained by aides in validation and redirection, not interpretation.
why_now: The post-war Soviet, Chinese, Caribbean and Southeast Asian immigrant cohorts who arrived in the 1960s-80s are now reaching moderate-to-severe dementia. Low-latency video is universal and cheap. AI companions such as KindredMind (voice clone of the caregiver, 12 languages, launched worldwide in May 2026) prove the demand, but they work best for mild cases and comfortable tech users. For moderate-to-severe dementia and live crises, the warm human voice in the right village dialect is the missing complement, and the agencies will pay per minute for it.
revenue_model: $1.25-1.75 per minute billed to agencies and plans, with 60-70 percent gross margin after specialist pay of about $0.45 per minute. Families get $129 per month for 20 sessions. Later, enterprise contracts with MLTC and D-SNP plans that cover the cost as a quality tool.
non_obvious_insight: Patients revert not just to a language but to a specific dialect and era, for example Toisanese, not Mandarin, and the idioms of 1955. A literal interpreter is useless because what calms is tone, a lullaby, a proverb and a familiar name. The buyer is not the family but the agency, which is desperate because language mismatch is why its aides quit its hardest cases. Nobody pays interpreters for companionship, so this talent pool of bilingual retirees is unmined and cheap.
first_30_days: Pick two languages with dense local demand, for example Toisanese or Cantonese in NYC and Haitian Creole in Miami. Recruit 10 bilingual retirees through churches, senior centers and community media. Train them in a one-page validation script. Run it on WhatsApp video with no software. Call 15 small agencies serving those communities and offer 30 free minutes per case. Sign the first three at $1.50 per minute with a $300 monthly minimum.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LanguageLine Solutions, Boostlingo, Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline, KindredMind (AI voice companion for caregiving families). White space: Caveat on confidence: WebSearch hit its session budget (200 of 200) before any of my searches ran. The verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches, not the 6-12 searches requested. I could not run the Crunchbase, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or YC queries. I also could not rule out a small direct competitor: a sub-$5M startup or a local agency-run in-language 'warm line' would not show up in these fetches. Within that limit, I found no product that puts a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's dialect on live video, speaking to the patient and coaching the English-speaking aide at the bedside. The gap is real but narrow. What remains unserved: (1) the crisis-moment human warm voice in long-tail dialects (Toisanese, Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Uzbek and similar) for moderate-to-severe patients; (2) a service sold per minute or per case to home care agencies and PACE programs rather than to families or employers; (3) validation and redirection training for bilingual retirees, where interpreters are trained to translate literally. Interpretation vendors are strong at language coverage and connect speed but have no dementia layer, and nothing stops them adding one. The Alzheimer's Association helpline is a free phone-only substitute. AI companions target mild cases. The main unproven parts are agency willingness to pay $1.25-1.75 per minute, and whether the Medicaid reimbursement structure lets agencies absorb it. At $1.50 per minute, a 6-minute session costs about $9, which is plausible per event, but agencies run on thin margins and no Medicaid code pays for it.

title: ITAR-Safe Identity for New-Space Startups
one_liner: An identity layer that proves a new hire is real, where they actually are and whether they may legally see spacecraft technical data, then feeds that attribute straight into SSO and PLM access controls.
customer: Series A-C launch, satellite and defense-space startups (50-500 staff) and their sub-tier machine shops and avionics suppliers, reached through space-focused investors, accelerators and SpaceWERX/SBIR cohorts. Buyers are the head of security or compliance and the CFO.
problem: Space startups are hiring at breakneck speed, with remote engineers and contractors, into a Golden Dome-driven market (cost estimate raised to $185B) and nine-figure funding rounds. Giving a foreign person access to technical data is an ITAR export violation, and North Korean IT-worker schemes have reached 70 to 100+ US companies. Standard IDV proves someone is real, not whether they are a US person, and HR and ATS tools do not carry export-control eligibility as an access attribute. Fake suppliers and counterfeit parts add a second exposure.
solution: (1) Verify person and US-person status using document and injection-resistant liveness (partner with an existing IDV vendor rather than building it). (2) Check presence over time (VPN and laptop-farm signals). (3) Write 'US person, permitted data categories' into Okta or Entra groups and PLM and repo permissions through SCIM. (4) Supplier onboarding with KYB, sanctions and counterfeit-part red flags. (5) An auditor-ready evidence pack for CMMC Level 2 assessments and export-compliance reviews.
why_now: The DoD's CMMC rollout reaches its second phase on 10 Nov 2026, when third-party Level 2 certification starts appearing in contracts, and small suppliers are scrambling. North Korean worker prosecutions in Apr and May 2026 put hiring fraud on boards' agendas, while 3-second voice cloning and virtual-camera injection attacks defeat casual video interviews.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified person per year, $1-3K per month platform fee, and $250 per supplier onboarding. Add a paid $2K 'ITAR access audit' as an entry product.
non_obvious_insight: In space the compliance object is not employee identity but nationality-scoped access to technical data. The unbuilt gap is attribute-based access control fed by identity proof into CAD and PLM systems. These startups fear DDTC and DoD audits and investor diligence more than hackers, so they buy compliance evidence rather than security.
first_30_days: Build a 'verified US person to Okta group' integration on an off-the-shelf IDV API. Sell a $2K ITAR access audit (export the Drive, GitHub and PLM permission lists and flag foreign-person exposures) to 5 startups via investor and accelerator introductions in Colorado Springs, Los Angeles and Huntsville. Convert audits to per-seat subscriptions before the Nov 2026 CMMC milestone.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: archTIS NC Protect, Persona (Candidate Verification), Incode Candidate Verification, Socure (workforce and candidate verification). White space: Verdict is gap, and a narrower one than the pitch implies. No product found does the specific loop the idea describes: proof of US-person status, the attribute written to an IdP through SCIM, enforcement in Drive, GitHub and PLM, and continuous drift detection. Four things fill the space today. IDV vendors (Persona, Incode, Socure, Nametag, CLEAR, Entra Verified ID) prove someone is real but do not assert or record ITAR eligibility. archTIS NC Protect enforces nationality-based access but only inside Microsoft 365 and file shares, and it trusts whatever attribute it is given. Managed-service shops (BEMO at about $4,800/month, ATX CMMC Space plus $30/user/month) deliver it as consulting with 8-month timelines. PLM vendors enforce access to an admin-typed attribute that no one has proven.

What is genuinely unserved:
- A lightweight, startup-priced system of record for US-person and permitted-data-category status, with the Empowered Official sign-off, that syncs to Okta, Entra and Google Workspace groups.
- Continuous deemed-export exposure scanning across the Drive, GitHub, Slack and PLM permission lists that startups actually use. Many are on commercial Google Workspace, which is not ITAR-compliant, and they cannot afford a GCC High or enclave migration.
- A managed workflow for licensed or TAA-scoped foreign-person exceptions, which is where hiring friction really sits.

Parts of the pitch that are not white space:
- Supplier KYB and counterfeit screening is owned by Exiger, Kharon and Sayari.
- CMMC evidence packs are owned by Secureframe, Vanta and Drata.
- Candidate and DPRK fraud detection is crowded and moving fast (Persona, Incode, Socure, Nametag, Endorsed).

Biggest structural risks:
1. The 'why now' is broken. DoD suspended CMMC Phase 2, due 10 Nov 2026, on 13 Jul 2026 and launched a 60-day reform review. Phase 1 self-assessments remain. Do not build the go-to-market around a Nov 2026 CMMC cliff.
2. Legal and product risk. The Clifford Chance settlement ($132K) shows DOJ IER penalizes employers who over-apply ITAR into citizenship discrimination. ITAR does not require hiring only US persons. Under INA 274B, employers cannot demand specific documents or run citizenship checks unevenly. A biometric 'US person' scanner sold to HR is legally delicate. Verifying green-card, asylee and refugee status by document scan is harder than a citizen passport check, and the I-9 already exists as the system of record.
3. Easy DIY. An IT admin can put an I-9-derived flag into an Okta group, so the paid value must be audit and drift detection plus the exception workflow, not the attribute itself.
4. Coverage limit. WebSearch is US-only and Crunchbase and YC searches surfaced nothing, so a stealth or very early startup on this exact wedge cannot be ruled out.
